evidence: src/application/dto/CreateOrderRequest.ts declares only the interfaces OrderItemInput { productId, quantity } and CreateOrderRequest { items: OrderItemInput[] }, which hold request data only.
src/application/dto/OrderResponse.ts declares OrderItemResponse and OrderResponse, and its state field reuses OrderStateType from the domain instead of redefining the states.
src/application/dto/ProductResponse.ts declares ProductResponse { id, name, availableStock, reservedStock, totalStock }, a data shape with no logic.
OrderItemInput and OrderItemResponse have the same fields, but they are separate request and response types, which is a common DTO convention and not a duplicated rule.
Each file has one importer: PlaceOrderUseCase imports CreateOrderRequest, ListOrdersByStateUseCase imports OrderResponse, and GetStockLevelsUseCase imports ProductResponse.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: This module passes. All three files hold only data-transfer interfaces for the application layer's use cases: one request DTO (CreateOrderRequest) and two response DTOs (OrderResponse, ProductResponse). They have no behaviour and contain no business rules or invariants that could be duplicated. OrderItemInput and OrderItemResponse have the same fields, but keeping input and output types separate is a common, deliberate pattern, not a copied invariant. ProductResponse includes totalStock alongside availableStock and reservedStock, but that field only describes the response's shape and computes nothing. OrderResponse reuses the domain type OrderStateType instead of redefining the order states, so it does not bypass an existing abstraction or duplicate the state list. Each file is imported by exactly one use case, which shows clear boundaries.
